prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

For example, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Bill of Rights include many elements within this functional area, especially when they focus on path- ways that are, “separate from trucks, buses and automobiles” (Breines & Dean, 1974). Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. One exception is the National Street Services more direct prescription for pedestrian’s “right to lower motorists’ speed.” Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s right to a “Street as a Safe Sanctuary” relates to all three of the above functional areas: Getting people safely across, along, and calming traffic speeds and flows (Appleyard et al., 1981). Likewise as referenced before there are many engineering strategies that have been used globally to facilitate more calm streets and related policies; from trees, to the number of windows, to appropriate modal separation to traffic flow (Ewing, Hajrasouliha, Neckerman, Purciel- Hill, & Greene, 2015). The modernist movement and functionalism provide many examples of how architects expose the use of the ramp and the lift. One of Le Corbusier’s arguments for the Marseilles Unité d`Habitation was precisely the rapid lifts that could move people fast vertically, “You will have an elevator in motion (rising or descending) every 40 ft., that is to say, in a few seconds.” And we find the ramp used for access both for the Bauhaus building by Walter Gropius in Berlin and in Oscar Niemeyer’s buildings in Niteroi near Rio de Janeiro. This idea of the “universal man” is based on an idea of a universal human being characterised by some universal measures of the body. This confirms that functionalism had no focus on social aspect The Barcelona model for pedestrian crossing was consistently used with the same design for more than 30 000 curb cuts over ten years. The Stockholm model looks a bit confusing and it is hard to call it a beautiful design. The London example shows a random use of paint and colour at the pedestrian crossing. In Japan, the use of tactile and visual guiding elements is a strong impulse in the visual landscape, for example in railway station in Kyoto. Have these ideas anything to do with the dilemmas of aesthetics and universal design as formulated in section 13 of the Norwegian Anti-Discrimination and Accessibility Act? Yes, it could quite easily indeed. Is contrast marking of stairs and handrails at two heights not very aesthetic? Poorly designed stairs and a lack of contrast marking on glass walls and doors cause several accidents, many of them very serious. 3. Much about Accessibility and Safety, but Little about Aesthetics and Architectural Heritage It is easy to understand the focus on accessibility and safety when working with the different juridical tools for the right for persons with some sort of impairment. Formulations such as removing manmade barriers of physical, economical and organizational character naturally have to use the accessibility views. It is easy to understand for everybody that the door must not be to narrow, that a single step in the floor or the pavement is a barrier for a person using a wheelchair. S.Asmervik/HowtoSolveDilemmasArisingfromtheIdeaofImprovingPhysicalAccessibility 93 After 50 years we know quite a lot about the use of wheelchairs. This knowledge is already implemented in standards, acts and regulations with measures of doors, turning circles for wheelchairs and design guidelines for stairs and ramps. And it is easy to register if a doorway is too narrow or a ramp too steep. And in USA at least can give you good reasons to sue someone and take them to court. More difficult with argument of aesthetics and architectural heritage. 4. Cultural Heritage Considerations There seems to be very different views on cultural heritage considerations in reaction to refurbishing historical monuments both indoors and outdoors in different countries and cities. {
  "scores": {
    "justice": {
      "overall": 61.0,
      "equity": 58.0,
      "fairness": 60.0,
      "accessibility": 65.0
    },
    "safety": 63.0,
    "livability": 60.0,
    "sustainability": 72.0,
    "aesthetics": 74.0,
    "comfort": 71.0,
    "walkability": 57.0
  },
  "explanations": {
    "justice": [
      "The lane appears to be shared by pedestrians and vehicles without a clearly marked sidewalk, so walking space is not distinctly protected or evenly allocated.",
      "The roadway is relatively narrow and low-speed in appearance, which can support fair shared use for all road users, but the lack of visible lane markings or designated pedestrian space limits clarity.",
      "The surface looks mostly level and continuous, with no obvious steps across the main path, which moderately supports accessibility for general users.",
      "No tactile paving, marked curb ramps, or other explicit barrier-free guidance elements are visible, so accessibility for a wide range of users is only partial."
    ],
    "safety": [
      "The street is narrow and enclosed by walls and trees, which likely slows vehicle speeds and reduces severe traffic conflict risk.",
      "Several pedestrians are standing directly at the edge of the carriageway, and because there is no separated sidewalk, pedestrian-vehicle interaction remains a safety concern.",
      "Dense tree canopy creates shade but also casts strong shadow patches on the pavement, which may reduce visibility of surface irregularities.",
      "There are no visible crosswalks, warning signs, or traffic-calming markings, so formal safety management appears limited."
    ],
    "livability": [
      "Large mature trees on both sides create a shaded, human-scaled environment that supports a calmer and more pleasant daily street experience.",
      "The presence of people standing and talking along the lane suggests some degree of social use and neighborhood familiarity.",
      "The setting appears quiet and low-traffic, which can support residential livability for everyday movement and informal interaction.",
      "However, there are no visible benches, storefronts, or public amenities, so the street offers limited support for longer stays or diverse activities."
    ],
    "sustainability": [
      "The mature tree canopy provides substantial greenery, which supports cooling, shade, and ecological value at the street level.",
      "The compact, narrow lane form may discourage high-speed driving and is compatible with lower-impact local access.",
      "Strong vegetation presence along both sides contributes more environmental benefit than a fully paved, exposed street would.",
      "No visible bike lane, transit stop, permeable paving, or stormwater infrastructure can be confirmed, so sustainability is helped mainly by the trees rather than multimodal facilities."
    ],
    "aesthetics": [
      "The arching tree canopy frames the lane and creates a visually attractive green corridor.",
      "Shade patterns from the trees add texture and visual depth to the otherwise simple paved surface.",
      "The modest walls and low-rise buildings create a quiet, intimate streetscape character rather than a harsh or oversized environment.",
      "Some surfaces and edges appear plain or worn, so the scene is pleasant mainly because of the vegetation rather than refined street design."
    ],
    "comfort": [
      "Extensive tree shade significantly improves thermal comfort by reducing direct sun exposure along much of the lane.",
      "The street appears relatively quiet and uncrowded, which supports psychological comfort for everyday passage.",
      "The pavement looks mostly continuous and navigable, offering moderate physical walking comfort for general users.",
      "Comfort is reduced by the absence of visible seating, dedicated pedestrian refuge space, or high-quality sidewalk paving."
    ],
    "walkability": [
      "The lane is short-scale, shaded, and likely low-speed, which supports basic walkability for local trips.",
      "Mature trees improve walking comfort by providing shade over much of the route.",
      "Walkability is weakened because pedestrians must share the same narrow paved space with vehicles, with no clearly separated sidewalk.",
      "There are no visible crossings, wayfinding elements, or pedestrian-priority markings, so the walking environment relies more on low traffic than on dedicated pedestrian design."
    ]
  }
}

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. In Japan, the use of tactile and visual guiding elements is a strong impulse in the visual landscape, for example in railway station in Kyoto. Have these ideas anything to do with the dilemmas of aesthetics and universal design as formulated in section 13 of the Norwegian Anti-Discrimination and Accessibility Act? Much about Accessibility and Safety, but Little about Aesthetics and Architectural Heritage It is easy to understand the focus on accessibility and safety when working with the different juridical tools for the right for persons with some sort of impairment. Formulations such as removing manmade barriers of physical, economical and organizational character naturally have to use the accessibility views. It is easy to understand for everybody that the door must not be to narrow, that a single step in the floor or the pavement is a barrier for a person using a wheelchair. S.Asmervik/HowtoSolveDilemmasArisingfromtheIdeaofImprovingPhysicalAccessibility 93 After 50 years we know quite a lot about the use of wheelchairs. This knowledge is already implemented in standards, acts and regulations with measures of doors, turning circles for wheelchairs and design guidelines for stairs and ramps. And it is easy to register if a doorway is too narrow or a ramp too steep. And in USA at least can give you good reasons to sue someone and take them to court. More difficult with argument of aesthetics and architectural heritage. 4.
